match.reason: No single bank point teaches the full set of factors that shift demand for the Australian dollar; the closest points cover only one or two of them (commodity prices, interest rates, or the basic supply-and-demand mechanism), so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Factors moving the exchange rate
card: The Australian dollar is priced by demand and supply in the foreign exchange market. Anything that raises demand for the dollar, or cuts its supply, tends to push it up. Anything that does the opposite pushes it down.
Interest rates
If Australian interest rates rise relative to those overseas, foreign investors want more Australian assets. They must buy dollars to do so, so demand for the dollar rises.
Exports and commodities

Higher world prices for Australian commodities, or stronger overseas demand for our exports, mean buyers need more dollars. Demand for the dollar rises. Stronger demand for imports means Australians sell dollars to buy foreign currency, so the dollar tends to fall.
Inflation and investment

Higher inflation in Australia than in partner countries makes our goods dearer, which cuts export demand and tends to lower the dollar. More foreign investment in Australia raises demand for the dollar.
draft.remember: Anything that makes foreigners want more Australian dollars lifts the exchange rate. Anything that makes Australians sell more dollars lowers it.

a.q: The Reserve Bank raises interest rates while rates in other major economies stay the same. What is the likely effect on the Australian dollar?
opts: Demand for it rises, so the dollar tends to appreciate
Demand for it falls, so the dollar tends to depreciate
Supply of it falls, so the dollar tends to depreciate
Nothing changes, as interest rates affect only borrowing
a.why: Higher Australian rates make Australian assets more attractive to foreign investors. They buy dollars to invest, so demand rises and the dollar tends to appreciate. The depreciation options reverse the cause and effect.
a.clue: Who needs to buy dollars when Australian returns look better?

b.q: Iron ore prices fall sharply, and overseas buyers order less from Perth miners. At the same time, Australian inflation runs above that of its trading partners. What is the likely effect on the dollar?
opts: It tends to fall, as both changes cut demand for it
It tends to rise, as lower prices make exports cheaper
It tends to rise, as higher inflation lifts demand for it
It stays steady, as the two changes cancel each other out
b.why: Lower commodity prices and weaker export orders mean buyers need fewer dollars. Higher relative inflation makes Australian goods dearer, which also cuts export demand. Both push the dollar down, so they do not cancel out.
b.clue: Check which way each change moves demand for dollars.

a.best: Demand for it rises, so the dollar tends to appreciate

b.best: It tends to fall, as both changes cut demand for it

problems.detail: The remember line splits the factors more neatly than the card does: foreigners buying dollars push it up, Australians selling dollars push it down. That misses cases the card teaches, such as higher Australian inflation, where foreigners want fewer dollars rather than Australians selling more. It also drops the card's 'tends to'.

The why says the depreciation options 'reverse the cause and effect'. That is not accurate. One gets the direction of demand wrong, and the other pairs a fall in supply with depreciation when a fall in supply would push the dollar up.

check.summary: The facts and both questions are sound, with one clear answer each. The remember line sorts the factors more neatly than the card and leaves out cases like relative inflation, and why (a) describes the wrong options inaccurately.
